patient.title: Pemetrexed + Cisplatin

agents.name: Pemetrexed
agents.explanation: Pemetrexed blocks several enzymes that use folate to make the building blocks of DNA and RNA. This can slow or stop cancer-cell growth. Healthy cells can also be affected. Prescribed folic acid and vitamin B12 reduce important toxicities and are part of treatment.
agents.watch: Take the prescribed folic acid and attend for B12. Report mouth sores, diarrhoea, a rash, breathlessness or reduced urine; check before taking ibuprofen or other non-prescription medicines.
risks: Low blood counts, infection and bleeding
Skin rash; rarely serious skin reactions

agents.name: Cisplatin
agents.explanation: Cisplatin forms links in DNA that interfere with copying and repair. This helps stop cancer cells dividing, but healthy tissues may also be affected. Kidney protection with fluids and monitoring is central to cisplatin treatment.
agents.watch: Report ringing in the ears, hearing changes, numbness or loss of function. Tell the team if you cannot drink, are passing less urine or become swollen or breathless during fluids.
risks: Low blood counts, infection and bleeding
Hearing changes or tinnitus, which can persist
Numbness or tingling, which can persist
Electrolyte changes and need for hydration

questions.q: Does having more side effects mean treatment is working?
questions.a: No. Side effects do not reliably show whether the cancer is responding. Report them so they can be treated. Your team assesses benefit using the tests and review plan appropriate to your cancer.

questions.q: Why might a dose be delayed or reduced?
questions.a: Your team may allow recovery, investigate a symptom or reduce the chance of lasting harm. Ask which drug changes, why, and when review is planned. A delay does not itself mean treatment has failed.

questions.q: What should I say when calling?
questions.a: Give the regimen name, last treatment date, symptoms and when they started. Explain whether you can eat, drink, pass urine and manage usual activities. Give your temperature if available, but do not delay calling to collect details.

questions.q: What belongs in the consent conversation?
questions.a: The individual aim and likely benefit, uncertainty, reasonable alternatives including not proceeding, common and serious risks, lasting effects, fertility and practical concerns. You can ask for an interpreter, more time or another explanation and can reconsider your decision.

questions.q: How many cycles should I use this passport for?
questions.a: The passport provides reusable recording pages, not a prescribed course length. Your oncology team sets the duration and can provide extra pages.

questions.q: Can I use this page to decide if blood results are safe?
questions.a: No. Treatment decisions require the clinical protocol, symptoms, previous toxicity, organ function and the prescriber’s review. The patient page explains the checks and does not authorise treatment.

questions.q: Is immunotherapy part of these two medicines?
questions.a: This guide covers pemetrexed and cisplatin chemotherapy. It does not include an immunotherapy medicine. If nivolumab, pembrolizumab or another medicine is also prescribed, obtain its separate regimen, consent, monitoring and emergency instructions. Mesothelioma and NSCLC have different aims and evidence; ask which indication is on your prescription.

questions.q: Will I always have four cycles?
questions.a: For pleural mesothelioma, the source describes up to 4–6 cycles. For advanced non-squamous NSCLC, it describes 4–6 combination cycles followed, when appropriate, by a separate pemetrexed maintenance plan (NCCP00222). The selected preoperative nivolumab combination uses three cycles and a separate immunotherapy plan (NCCP00849). Your team confirms which course applies and may stop or change it earlier.

questions.q: Why take vitamins during chemotherapy?
questions.a: Folic acid and vitamin B12 lower important pemetrexed side effects. They are prescribed parts of this regimen. Tell the team promptly if they were missed.

questions.q: What happens when the platinum chemotherapy stops?
questions.a: The next step depends on your disease and treatment aim. Selected advanced NSCLC plans may move to pemetrexed maintenance under a separate regimen. Preoperative treatment leads to a surgical-team review; mesothelioma follow-up is agreed with the oncology team.

questions.q: What should I be able to explain before I leave?
questions.a: Ask your nurse or doctor to check that you can explain which medicines you are receiving, the treatment days, which medicines to take at home, and which number to ring urgently. Ask for the plan in writing if any part is unclear.

chapters.title: Understanding your treatment
chapters.intro: The same chemotherapy pair appears in more than one disease setting.

items.title: Confirm the indication
items.text: Pemetrexed + Cisplatin is chemotherapy used for selected people with unresectable pleural mesothelioma or non-squamous non-small-cell lung cancer. The aim may be disease control or, within a separate combined preoperative plan, support for surgery. Ask your team to explain the expected benefit for your own diagnosis.

items.title: This guide’s scope
items.text: This summary covers the two chemotherapy medicines. If nivolumab is part of your treatment before surgery, use the full nivolumab combination plan. The nivolumab combination has its own side effects, monitoring and urgent advice; it is not covered by a chemotherapy-only handout. Ask your team to confirm whether the plan is for mesothelioma, advanced non-squamous lung cancer or treatment before surgery.

chapters.title: Before the first treatment
chapters.intro: Preparation reduces avoidable risk and makes the plan clearer.

items.title: Blood tests and kidney assessment
items.text: Baseline checks include full blood count, kidney and liver tests. The team also reviews the cisplatin hydration plan and existing kidney problems.

items.title: Nerves and hearing
items.text: Describe any numbness, weakness, ringing in the ears or hearing difficulty before starting. A hearing test is arranged when clinically indicated.

items.title: Vitamins, steroids and medicines
items.text: Confirm that folic acid has started, B12 was given, and you have one clear steroid and anti-sickness prescription. Bring a complete medicines list.

items.title: Consent and priorities
items.text: Confirm the treatment aim and indication, likely benefit and uncertainty, reasonable alternatives including not proceeding, serious and lasting risks, kidney/hearing/nerve problems, fertility and pregnancy advice, vitamin and steroid plans, and the chance of delays or dose changes.

chapters.title: What happens on treatment day
chapters.intro: The infusion times are only part of your visit.

items.title: Assessment first
items.text: Blood results and symptoms are reviewed before a dose is authorised. A delay or reduction may allow recovery and reduce lasting harm.

items.title: Your infusions
items.text: Pemetrexed is given into a vein over about 10 minutes, followed by cisplatin over about 60 minutes, starting 30 minutes after pemetrexed. Fluids before and after cisplatin make the visit longer; the team individualises hydration and electrolyte replacement. The whole visit also includes blood-result review, prevention medicines, preparation and observation.

items.title: During the infusion
items.text: Tell the nurse immediately about feeling unwell, breathing difficulty, itching, swelling, pain, burning or redness around the drip. Do not wait to see whether it settles.

chapters.title: Looking after yourself between visits
chapters.intro: Ask for help early with symptoms and practical difficulties.

items.title: Symptoms and daily life
items.text: Rest when needed while keeping activity manageable. Ask for nutrition, fatigue, work, transport or financial support. Keep a short symptom record for review.

items.title: Mouth and bowel care
items.text: Follow the team’s mouth-care plan. Report painful swallowing, persistent diarrhoea, vomiting or difficulty maintaining fluids; severe symptoms need urgent advice.

items.title: Hearing and nerves
items.text: Report tinnitus, hearing change, numbness or difficulty with everyday tasks before further treatment. These effects can persist after treatment ends.

items.title: Fertility, pregnancy and breastfeeding
items.text: Discuss fertility preservation, contraception and pregnancy plans before treatment. Pregnancy and breastfeeding are exclusions in the regimen. Ask the team for the medicine-specific contraception period.

chapters.title: When to get urgent help
chapters.intro: Use your unit’s 24-hour advice number and emergency instructions.

items.title: Possible infection
items.text: Call immediately for the fever threshold your unit gives you, shaking chills or sudden illness. You can have a serious infection without a high temperature. Do not wait for the next appointment.

items.title: Other urgent changes
items.text: Call urgently for fever or shaking chills, sudden illness, new or worsening breathlessness, chest pain, uncontrolled bleeding, severe or persistent diarrhoea, inability to drink, very little urine, a spreading or blistering rash, or swelling/wheeze during an infusion. Tell the team promptly about new tinnitus, hearing change, numbness, weakness or difficulty walking.

items.title: When you call
items.text: Give your medicines, last treatment date and symptoms. Explain whether you can drink and pass urine. If emergency help is needed, follow local emergency instructions and tell staff you are receiving chemotherapy.

chapters.title: Review, completion and a possible next phase
chapters.intro: The plan changes according to benefit, recovery and your priorities.

items.title: Response assessment
items.text: Scans and other tests are timed by the consultant’s treatment plan. Symptoms and side effects alone do not show whether treatment is working.

day_groups.body: Continue folic acid and the prescribed anti-sickness medicines. Your team combines the pemetrexed rash steroid and anti-sickness steroid into one clear schedule.

day_groups.body: Fatigue, bowel or mouth symptoms and low blood counts may develop between visits. Nerve or hearing symptoms can build across cycles.

support.title: Folic acid every day
support.text: The source uses 350–1000 micrograms daily: at least five doses during the seven days before the first pemetrexed, throughout treatment and for 21 days after the last pemetrexed. Follow your own prescription and tell the team about missed doses.

support.title: Vitamin B12 injection
support.text: The source uses 1000 micrograms into a muscle during the week before the first pemetrexed, then every three cycles. Later injections can be on treatment day. Confirm who books them.

support.title: One steroid schedule
support.text: Pemetrexed rash prevention uses dexamethasone-equivalent 4 mg twice daily on the day before, day of and day after treatment. The anti-sickness plan also uses steroids. Your prescriber/pharmacist must provide one reconciled schedule; do not add two courses together.

support.title: Preventing and treating sickness
support.text: This cisplatin combination has high sickness risk. Take prevention medicines as prescribed even when you feel well, and keep the team’s rescue plan available. The usual high-risk reference includes olanzapine; ask about sleepiness, falls and interactions.

support.title: Fluids and kidney protection
support.text: Ask for an individual drinking plan, especially with heart or kidney problems. Report inability to drink or reduced urine. Cisplatin needs supervised fluids before and after treatment; additional salts may be prescribed.

support.title: Medicines and self-care
support.text: Check all prescriptions, painkillers, supplements and vaccines with the oncology team. Some anti-inflammatory medicines can affect pemetrexed clearance; do not start or stop them on this guide’s authority. Follow mouth-care and infection advice.

evidence.title: Evidence depends on the cancer and the exact medicines
evidence.intro: Ask which study and treatment aim match your situation.
evidence.population: Pleural mesothelioma and advanced NSCLC were studied in different trials.
evidence.interpretation: In unresectable pleural mesothelioma, a randomised study found better survival with pemetrexed plus cisplatin than cisplatin alone. A different advanced NSCLC trial compared cisplatin/pemetrexed with cisplatin/gemcitabine; benefit differed by tumour histology, supporting non-squamous selection. These studies cannot predict an individual outcome, and neither describes standalone neoadjuvant immunotherapy.

chronology_notes.title: No safe-day prediction
chronology_notes.text: Low counts or serious symptoms can occur between visits. The position in the cycle never rules out infection or another urgent problem.

chronology_notes.title: Across the course
chronology_notes.text: Nerve, hearing and kidney effects can accumulate or persist. The number of cycles and any transition to maintenance depend on the indication and consultant review.

patient.title: Pemetrexed + Carboplatin

agents.name: Pemetrexed
agents.explanation: Pemetrexed blocks several enzymes that use folate to make the building blocks of DNA and RNA. This can slow or stop cancer-cell growth. Healthy cells can also be affected. Prescribed folic acid and vitamin B12 reduce important toxicities and are part of treatment.
agents.watch: Take the prescribed folic acid and attend for B12. Report mouth sores, diarrhoea, a rash, breathlessness or reduced urine; check before taking ibuprofen or other non-prescription medicines.
risks: Low blood counts, infection and bleeding
Skin rash; rarely serious skin reactions

agents.name: Carboplatin
agents.explanation: Carboplatin forms links in DNA that interfere with copying and repair. This helps stop cancer cells dividing, but healthy tissues may also be affected. The dose is tailored using kidney function because the kidneys clear carboplatin.
agents.watch: Report ringing in the ears, hearing changes, numbness or loss of function. Report infection or unusual bruising/bleeding promptly and describe any symptoms during the infusion.
risks: Low blood counts, infection and bleeding
Hearing changes or tinnitus, which can persist
Numbness or tingling, which can persist

questions.q: Does having more side effects mean treatment is working?
questions.a: No. Side effects do not reliably show whether the cancer is responding. Report them so they can be treated. Your team assesses benefit using the tests and review plan appropriate to your cancer.

questions.q: Why might a dose be delayed or reduced?
questions.a: Your team may allow recovery, investigate a symptom or reduce the chance of lasting harm. Ask which drug changes, why, and when review is planned. A delay does not itself mean treatment has failed.

questions.q: What should I say when calling?
questions.a: Give the regimen name, last treatment date, symptoms and when they started. Explain whether you can eat, drink, pass urine and manage usual activities. Give your temperature if available, but do not delay calling to collect details.

questions.q: What belongs in the consent conversation?
questions.a: The individual aim and likely benefit, uncertainty, reasonable alternatives including not proceeding, common and serious risks, lasting effects, fertility and practical concerns. You can ask for an interpreter, more time or another explanation and can reconsider your decision.

questions.q: How many cycles should I use this passport for?
questions.a: The passport provides reusable recording pages, not a prescribed course length. Your oncology team sets the duration and can provide extra pages.

questions.q: Can I use this page to decide if blood results are safe?
questions.a: No. Treatment decisions require the clinical protocol, symptoms, previous toxicity, organ function and the prescriber’s review. The patient page explains the checks and does not authorise treatment.

questions.q: Is immunotherapy part of these two medicines?
questions.a: This guide covers pemetrexed and carboplatin chemotherapy. It does not include an immunotherapy medicine. If nivolumab, pembrolizumab or another medicine is also prescribed, obtain its separate regimen, consent, monitoring and emergency instructions. Mesothelioma and NSCLC have different aims and evidence; ask which indication is on your prescription.

questions.q: Will I always have four cycles?
questions.a: For pleural mesothelioma, the source describes up to 4–6 cycles. For advanced non-squamous NSCLC, it describes 4–6 combination cycles followed, when appropriate, by a separate pemetrexed maintenance plan (NCCP00222). The selected preoperative nivolumab combination uses three cycles and a separate immunotherapy plan (NCCP00849). Your team confirms which course applies and may stop or change it earlier.

questions.q: Why take vitamins during chemotherapy?
questions.a: Folic acid and vitamin B12 lower important pemetrexed side effects. They are prescribed parts of this regimen. Tell the team promptly if they were missed.

questions.q: What happens when the platinum chemotherapy stops?
questions.a: The next step depends on your disease and treatment aim. Selected advanced NSCLC plans may move to pemetrexed maintenance under a separate regimen. Preoperative treatment leads to a surgical-team review; mesothelioma follow-up is agreed with the oncology team.

questions.q: What should I be able to explain before I leave?
questions.a: Ask your nurse or doctor to check that you can explain which medicines you are receiving, the treatment days, which medicines to take at home, and which number to ring urgently. Ask for the plan in writing if any part is unclear.

items.title: Confirm the indication
items.text: Pemetrexed + Carboplatin is chemotherapy used for selected people with unresectable pleural mesothelioma or non-squamous non-small-cell lung cancer. The aim may be disease control or, within a separate combined preoperative plan, support for surgery. Ask your team to explain the expected benefit for your own diagnosis.

items.title: This guide’s scope
items.text: This summary covers the two chemotherapy medicines. If nivolumab is part of your treatment before surgery, use the full nivolumab combination plan. The nivolumab combination has its own side effects, monitoring and urgent advice; it is not covered by a chemotherapy-only handout. Ask your team to confirm whether the plan is for mesothelioma, advanced non-squamous lung cancer or treatment before surgery.

chapters.title: Before the first treatment
chapters.intro: Preparation reduces avoidable risk and makes the plan clearer.

items.title: Blood tests and kidney assessment
items.text: Baseline checks include full blood count, kidney and liver tests. An isotope GFR measurement is preferred where feasible; a validated estimate may be used.

items.title: Nerves and hearing
items.text: Describe any numbness, weakness, ringing in the ears or hearing difficulty before starting. A hearing test is arranged when clinically indicated.

items.title: Vitamins, steroids and medicines
items.text: Confirm that folic acid has started, B12 was given, and you have one clear steroid and anti-sickness prescription. Bring a complete medicines list.

items.title: Consent and priorities
items.text: Confirm the treatment aim and indication, likely benefit and uncertainty, reasonable alternatives including not proceeding, serious and lasting risks, kidney/hearing/nerve problems, fertility and pregnancy advice, vitamin and steroid plans, and the chance of delays or dose changes. chapters.title: What happens on treatment day
chapters.intro: The infusion times are only part of your visit.

items.title: Assessment first
items.text: Blood results and symptoms are reviewed before a dose is authorised. A delay or reduction may allow recovery and reduce lasting harm.

items.title: Your infusions
items.text: Pemetrexed is given into a vein over about 10 minutes, followed by carboplatin over about 30 minutes. Carboplatin dosing uses a verified kidney-function measure; the dose may change when kidney function changes. The whole visit also includes blood-result review, prevention medicines, preparation and observation.

items.title: During the infusion
items.text: Tell the nurse immediately about feeling unwell, breathing difficulty, itching, swelling, pain, burning or redness around the drip. Do not wait to see whether it settles.

chapters.title: Looking after yourself between visits
chapters.intro: Ask for help early with symptoms and practical difficulties.

items.title: Symptoms and daily life
items.text: Rest when needed while keeping activity manageable. Ask for nutrition, fatigue, work, transport or financial support. Keep a short symptom record for review.

items.title: Mouth and bowel care
items.text: Follow the team’s mouth-care plan. Report painful swallowing, persistent diarrhoea, vomiting or difficulty maintaining fluids; severe symptoms need urgent advice.

items.title: Hearing and nerves
items.text: Report tinnitus, hearing change, numbness or difficulty with everyday tasks before further treatment. These effects can persist after treatment ends.

items.title: Fertility, pregnancy and breastfeeding
items.text: Discuss fertility preservation, contraception and pregnancy plans before treatment. Pregnancy and breastfeeding are exclusions in the regimen. Ask the team for the medicine-specific contraception period.

chapters.title: When to get urgent help
chapters.intro: Use your unit’s 24-hour advice number and emergency instructions.

items.title: Possible infection
items.text: Call immediately for the fever threshold your unit gives you, shaking chills or sudden illness. You can have a serious infection without a high temperature. Do not wait for the next appointment.

items.title: Other urgent changes
items.text: Call urgently for fever or shaking chills, sudden illness, new or worsening breathlessness, chest pain, uncontrolled bleeding, severe or persistent diarrhoea, inability to drink, very little urine, a spreading or blistering rash, or swelling/wheeze during an infusion. Tell the team promptly about new tinnitus, hearing change, numbness, weakness or difficulty walking.

items.title: When you call
items.text: Give your medicines, last treatment date and symptoms. Explain whether you can drink and pass urine. If emergency help is needed, follow local emergency instructions and tell staff you are receiving chemotherapy.

chapters.title: Review, completion and a possible next phase
chapters.intro: The plan changes according to benefit, recovery and your priorities.

items.title: Response assessment

support.text: The source uses 350–1000 micrograms daily: at least five doses during the seven days before the first pemetrexed, throughout treatment and for 21 days after the last pemetrexed. Follow your own prescription and tell the team about missed doses.

support.text: The source uses 1000 micrograms into a muscle during the week before the first pemetrexed, then every three cycles. Later injections can be on treatment day. Confirm who books them.

support.text: Pemetrexed rash prevention uses dexamethasone-equivalent 4 mg twice daily on the day before, day of and day after treatment. The anti-sickness plan also uses steroids. Your prescriber/pharmacist must provide one reconciled schedule; do not add two courses together.

support.title: Preventing and treating sickness
support.text: This carboplatin combination has high sickness risk. Take prevention medicines as prescribed even when you feel well, and keep the team’s rescue plan available. Carboplatin AUC5 has a dedicated anti-sickness plan; do not automatically copy another high-risk chemotherapy plan.

support.title: Fluids and kidney protection
support.text: Ask for an individual drinking plan, especially with heart or kidney problems. Report inability to drink or reduced urine. Kidney tests help the team set the carboplatin dose. Extra tests may be needed after dehydration or a change in health.

support.title: Medicines and self-care
support.text: Check all prescriptions, painkillers, supplements and vaccines with the oncology team. Some anti-inflammatory medicines can affect pemetrexed clearance; do not start or stop them on this guide’s authority. Follow mouth-care and infection advice.

evidence.title: Evidence depends on the cancer and the exact medicines
evidence.intro: Ask which study and treatment aim match your situation.
evidence.population: Pleural mesothelioma and advanced NSCLC were studied in different trials.
evidence.interpretation: In advanced NSCLC, a randomised study found similar reported quality of life and survival with pemetrexed/carboplatin and gemcitabine/carboplatin, with less blood-count toxicity in the pemetrexed group. Mesothelioma evidence includes a smaller study without a randomised comparator. Cisplatin trial survival figures cannot be assigned to carboplatin. Your team should explain which evidence matches your diagnosis and alternatives.

patient.title: Carboplatin + Etoposide

agents.name: Carboplatin
agents.explanation: Carboplatin forms links in DNA that interfere with copying and repair. This helps stop cancer cells dividing; normal tissues can also be affected. Carboplatin dosing is tailored using a verified kidney-function result; low blood counts can be an important limiting effect.
agents.watch: Report changes in urine, hearing, ringing in the ears, numbness or daily function. Tell the team about infection, unusual bruising or bleeding and any symptoms during the infusion.
risks: Low blood counts, infection and bleeding
Effects on fertility and harm to an unborn baby
Hearing changes or tinnitus, which may persist

agents.name: Etoposide
agents.mechanism: Disrupts DNA repair during cell division
agents.explanation: Etoposide interferes with topoisomerase II, an enzyme that helps manage DNA during copying. DNA breaks can remain unrepaired and cancer cells may stop dividing or die. Healthy cells are also affected; the infusion or prescribed capsules deliver the same medicine by different routes.
agents.watch: Report fever, bleeding, mouth sores or diarrhoea. Tell the nurse about faintness, rash or breathing difficulty during an infusion. If capsules are prescribed, use the exact pharmacy instructions and contact the team about a missed or vomited dose.
risks: Low blood counts, infection and bleeding

questions.q: Why are there three treatment days?
questions.a: Etoposide is planned on three consecutive days. Usually you attend for infusions on all three. The alternative capsule plan is only used when prescribed and clearly labelled by your team.

questions.q: Are etoposide capsules the same dose as the drip?
questions.a: No. The source oral alternative has a different dose and twice-daily schedule. Your prescription and pharmacy label specify your individual dose and capsule strengths. Do not convert it yourself.

questions.q: Will I have radiotherapy or immunotherapy too?
questions.a: This guide covers Carboplatin + Etoposide chemotherapy for extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer. Immunotherapy combinations and limited-stage treatment with radiotherapy use separate regimens. If an additional medicine or radiotherapy is prescribed, obtain its own plan and consent information.

questions.q: How long does the course last?
questions.a: The source describes 4–6 cycles every 21 days, or stopping for cancer progression or unacceptable side effects. Your team confirms the intended course and may change it earlier. The passport pages are reusable records, not a prescription for a fixed number of visits.

questions.q: Do more side effects mean treatment is working?
questions.a: No. Side effects do not reliably show whether the cancer is responding. Report them so they can be assessed and treated; your team reviews benefit with the agreed clinical and scan plan.

questions.q: Why might treatment be delayed or changed?
questions.a: Blood counts, kidney/liver function or symptoms may need time to recover. A dose may change to reduce lasting harm. Ask which medicine changes, why, and when it will be reviewed.

questions.q: What should I say when I call?
questions.a: Give the regimen name, last treatment day, symptoms and when they started. Explain whether you can drink, pass urine and manage usual activities. Give your temperature if available, but do not delay calling to collect information.

questions.q: Can this guide decide whether treatment is safe?
questions.a: No. Treatment decisions need your clinical results, symptoms, previous toxicity and prescriber/pharmacy review. This guide helps you understand and discuss the plan.

questions.q: What should I be able to explain before I leave?
questions.a: Ask your nurse or doctor to check that you can explain which medicines you are receiving, the treatment days, which medicines to take at home, and which number to ring urgently. Ask for the plan in writing if any part is unclear.

evidence.title: Evidence and your own treatment decision
evidence.intro: The exact medicines, dose, population and treatment era matter.
evidence.population: Extensive-stage SCLC; JCOG9702 specifically enrolled elderly or poor-risk patients.
evidence.interpretation: Platinum and etoposide are established chemotherapy components for extensive-stage SCLC. A pooled comparison found no clear survival difference between carboplatin-based and cisplatin-based treatment, but their side effects differed. The elderly/poor-risk JCOG9702 trial used etoposide 80 mg/m² and split cisplatin, so its survival figures cannot be assigned directly to this 100 mg/m² etoposide schedule. These older chemotherapy comparisons do not rank current immunotherapy combinations or predict an individual outcome.

chapters.title: Your treatment and its aim

items.title: The treatment covered here
items.text: This summary is for chemotherapy for extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer. Treatment that also includes immunotherapy or radiotherapy needs its own complete plan.

items.title: Why two medicines?
items.text: The platinum drug damages DNA and etoposide interferes with DNA repair. Using them together attacks cell growth in different ways. Healthy cells can also be affected.

items.title: Evidence and choices
items.text: Platinum and etoposide are established chemotherapy components for extensive-stage SCLC. A pooled comparison found no clear survival difference between carboplatin-based and cisplatin-based treatment, but their side effects differed. The elderly/poor-risk JCOG9702 trial used etoposide 80 mg/m² and split cisplatin, so its survival figures cannot be assigned directly to this 100 mg/m² etoposide schedule. These older chemotherapy comparisons do not rank current immunotherapy combinations or predict an individual outcome.

chapters.title: Before treatment
chapters.intro: Preparation helps the team choose a suitable plan.

items.title: Tests and fitness
items.text: Blood counts, kidney and liver tests are checked before treatment. Tell the team about existing nerve/hearing problems, other medicines and any recent infection.

items.title: Route and practical arrangements
items.text: Confirm whether all three etoposide doses are infusions or whether you have capsules on Days 2 and 3. Do not substitute one route yourself.

items.title: Fertility, contraception and pregnancy
items.text: Discuss fertility preservation and contraception before treatment. Pregnancy and breastfeeding are exclusions. Ask for medicine-specific advice and the required contraception period.

chapters.title: Your visits and home plan
chapters.intro: Three treatment days form one cycle.

items.title: Day 1
items.text: Carboplatin is infused over about 30 minutes, followed by etoposide over about one hour on Day 1. Etoposide alone is given on Days 2 and 3 unless the prescribed capsule alternative is selected. The whole visit also includes review, preparation, prevention medicines and observation.

items.title: Days 2 and 3
items.text: Continue etoposide by the prescribed route, with risk-appropriate anti-sickness prevention each treatment day.

items.title: The following days
items.text: Continue only the written prevention schedule and monitor symptoms. The two days after the final treatment day are part of the multi-day antiemetic review.

chapters.title: Effects to discuss and monitor
chapters.intro: Report problems early; they are not a measure of benefit.

items.title: Blood counts and infection
items.text: Both medicines may lower blood counts. Infection can become serious quickly; follow the urgent advice plan for fever, chills or sudden illness.

items.title: Hearing, nerves and kidneys
items.text: Platinum medicines may affect hearing, nerves and kidneys, and some changes can last. Tell the team promptly about tinnitus, hearing change, numbness or reduced urine.

items.title: Mouth, bowel, hair and fatigue
items.text: Mouth soreness, nausea, bowel changes, hair loss and tiredness can affect daily life. Ask for help with symptoms; call urgently if you cannot drink or symptoms are severe.

items.title: Later effects
items.text: Etoposide can be associated with a later blood cancer. Discuss serious and lasting risks together with likely benefit and alternatives.

chapters.title: When to seek urgent help
chapters.intro: Use your unit’s 24-hour number and emergency instructions.

items.title: Urgent symptoms
items.text: Call urgently for fever or shaking chills, sudden illness, new or worsening breathlessness, chest pain, uncontrolled bleeding, severe diarrhoea, vomiting despite medicines, inability to drink, very little urine, or a spreading/blistering rash. Tell staff immediately about wheeze, swelling, dizziness or faintness during an infusion. Report hearing changes, ringing in the ears, numbness, weakness or difficulty walking promptly.

items.title: When calling
items.text: Give your regimen, last treatment day and symptoms. Explain whether you can drink and pass urine. Do not wait for the next appointment or for a high temperature if you feel very unwell.

agents.name: Etoposide
agents.mechanism: Disrupts DNA repair during cell division
agents.explanation: Etoposide interferes with topoisomerase II, an enzyme that helps manage DNA during copying. DNA breaks can remain unrepaired and cancer cells may stop dividing or die. Healthy cells are also affected; the infusion or prescribed capsules deliver the same medicine by different routes.
agents.watch: Report fever, bleeding, mouth sores or diarrhoea. Tell the nurse about faintness, rash or breathing difficulty during an infusion. If capsules are prescribed, use the exact pharmacy instructions and contact the team about a missed or vomited dose.

agents.name: Cisplatin
agents.explanation: Cisplatin forms links in DNA that interfere with copying and repair. This helps stop cancer cells dividing; normal tissues can also be affected. Kidney protection and assessment of hearing and nerves are essential during cisplatin treatment.
agents.watch: Report changes in urine, hearing, ringing in the ears, numbness or daily function. Tell the team about infection, unusual bruising or bleeding and any symptoms during the infusion.

questions.q: Why are there three treatment days?
questions.a: Etoposide is planned on three consecutive days. Usually you attend for infusions on all three. The alternative capsule plan is only used when prescribed and clearly labelled by your team.

questions.q: Are etoposide capsules the same dose as the drip?
questions.a: No. The source oral alternative has a different dose and twice-daily schedule. Your prescription and pharmacy label specify your individual dose and capsule strengths. Do not convert it yourself.

questions.q: Will I have radiotherapy or immunotherapy too?
questions.a: This guide covers Cisplatin + Etoposide chemotherapy for extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer. Immunotherapy combinations and limited-stage treatment with radiotherapy use separate regimens. If an additional medicine or radiotherapy is prescribed, obtain its own plan and consent information.

questions.q: How long does the course last?
questions.a: The source plans 4–6 cycles, usually every 21 days. The team may delay, reduce or stop treatment according to your health and response. The passport pages are reusable records, not a prescription for a fixed number of visits.

questions.q: Do more side effects mean treatment is working?
questions.a: No. Side effects do not reliably show whether the cancer is responding. Report them so they can be assessed and treated; your team reviews benefit with the agreed clinical and scan plan.

questions.q: Why might treatment be delayed or changed?
questions.a: Blood counts, kidney/liver function or symptoms may need time to recover. A dose may change to reduce lasting harm. Ask which medicine changes, why, and when it will be reviewed.

questions.q: What should I say when I call?
questions.a: Give the regimen name, last treatment day, symptoms and when they started. Explain whether you can drink, pass urine and manage usual activities. Give your temperature if available, but do not delay calling to collect information.

questions.q: Can this guide decide whether treatment is safe?
questions.a: No. Treatment decisions need your clinical results, symptoms, previous toxicity and prescriber/pharmacy review. This guide helps you understand and discuss the plan.

questions.q: What should I be able to explain before I leave?
questions.a: Ask your nurse or doctor to check that you can explain which medicines you are receiving, the treatment days, which medicines to take at home, and which number to ring urgently. Ask for the plan in writing if any part is unclear.

items.title: The treatment covered here
items.text: This summary is for chemotherapy for extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer. Treatment that also includes immunotherapy or radiotherapy needs its own complete plan.

items.title: Why two medicines?
items.text: The platinum drug damages DNA and etoposide interferes with DNA repair. Using them together attacks cell growth in different ways. Healthy cells can also be affected.

items.title: Evidence and choices
items.text: Platinum and etoposide are established chemotherapy components for extensive-stage SCLC. A pooled comparison found no clear survival difference between carboplatin-based and cisplatin-based treatment, but their side effects differed. The elderly/poor-risk JCOG9702 trial used etoposide 80 mg/m² and split cisplatin, so its survival figures cannot be assigned directly to this 100 mg/m² etoposide schedule. These older chemotherapy comparisons do not rank current immunotherapy combinations or predict an individual outcome.

items.title: Route and practical arrangements

items.title: Day 1
items.text: Etoposide is infused over about one hour before cisplatin, which is infused over about one hour on Day 1. Extra IV fluid and electrolytes before/after cisplatin make this a longer visit. items.title: Days 2 and 3
items.text: Continue etoposide by the prescribed route, with risk-appropriate anti-sickness prevention each treatment day.

items.title: The following days
items.text: Continue only the written prevention schedule and monitor symptoms. The two days after the final treatment day are part of the multi-day antiemetic review.

chapters.title: Effects to discuss and monitor
chapters.intro: Report problems early; they are not a measure of benefit.

items.title: Blood counts and infection
items.text: Both medicines may lower blood counts. Infection can become serious quickly; follow the urgent advice plan for fever, chills or sudden illness.

items.title: Hearing, nerves and kidneys
items.text: Platinum medicines may affect hearing, nerves and kidneys, and some changes can last. Tell the team promptly about tinnitus, hearing change, numbness or reduced urine.

items.title: Mouth, bowel, hair and fatigue
items.text: Mouth soreness, nausea, bowel changes, hair loss and tiredness can affect daily life. Ask for help with symptoms; call urgently if you cannot drink or symptoms are severe.

items.title: Later effects
items.text: Etoposide can be associated with a later blood cancer. Discuss serious and lasting risks together with likely benefit and alternatives.
